speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: asked the Prime Minister (a) in the last six months, whether there is an increase in successful bank-related cyber scams or unauthorised bank transactions involving victims not divulging their OTPs, IDs or passwords to scammers; (b) who bears the financial loss when the unauthorised transaction is not due to the banks’ lapses or non-compliance with Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) rules and the consumer has not given his login information to a third party; and (c) whether victims who suffer financial loss can be given financial help during the period of investigation and recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For unauthorised transactions exceeding this limit, financial institutions will investigate further on the root cause of the issue before liability is established.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Where the unauthorised transaction arose because of lapses or non-compliance with MAS’ rules by the financial institution, the consumer will not be liable.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The question raised by Ms Yeo pertains to a situation where neither the consumer nor the financial institution is at fault.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Specifically, the consumer has not given out his credentials to a scammer and there were no lapses or non-compliance on the part of the financial institution.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Between September 2020 and February 2021, the Singapore Police Force (SPF) received a total of 89 reports of fraudulent card transactions performed with SMS OTPs, where victims claimed that they neither performed the transactions nor received any SMS OTPs to authorise the transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: While these cases represent less than 0.1% of fraudulent online card transactions reported and the number of cases has come down since March 2021, it is nonetheless concerning.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: SPF and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) are investigating these cases.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS has however asked financial institutions to step up vigilance towards such fraud.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Financial institutions have put in place additional measures, such as rejecting card payments made to common merchants previously linked to the unauthorised transactions or placing limits on the transaction amounts that consumers can transact with such merchants.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS also expects financial institutions to ensure that consumers are treated fairly whilst investigations are ongoing.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For instance, banks have waived finance charges and late fees on the outstanding amounts or offered temporary goodwill credits on the consumers’ credit cards in the interim.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For those who wish to settle on the issue, banks may also offer partial waiver of the disputed amounts, taking into consideration individual circumstances, such as financial hardship and whether there were indicators of negligence by the consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS is working with the industry to review the existing framework to provide greater clarity on the responsibilities and liabilities of consumers and financial institutions in the case of fraudulent payment transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The review will include the scenario where neither the consumer nor the financial institution was remiss in allowing the fraud to occur, the scenario that Ms Yeo had asked about.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The framework should provide a balance of incentives for all parties to do their part in preventing fraudulent transactions, while ensuring that consumers who are not at fault are protected.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have seen over the past few months a rise in the number of appeal cases from my residents who have fallen victim to such cyber crimes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They tell me that they have not received any OTPs nor have they divulged their bank account information or credit card information unwittingly.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When they go to their banks for investigation, their banks' usual response is that they have divulged their OTPs and hence, the victim, not the bank, is responsible for the loss.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of my residents, who is a retiree, lost over $10,000 in a string of transactions and she is very sure that she has never given her OTP once, if any.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another resident has told me he has merely done one banking transaction online with a payment platform and before he knew it, he had $1,000 missing from his bank account.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the push towards online financial transactions and digital banking, what are the measures that the Ministry has put in place, especially with the banks and financial institutions, to ensure that our citizens are made aware of these fast-evolving banking and credit card scams?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am sorry to hear about her residents who have been victims of these fraud cases.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I cited just now in my reply, if you look at the overall statistics, the numbers have not been rising and the overall numbers are small as a percentage of transactions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Nevertheless, as I highlighted, this is concerning and we are doing a few things.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Two, MAS has also asked the financial institutions to step up vigilance, as I highlighted just now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, they are putting in place additional measures, including making consumers more aware of such possible frauds that may happen.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the banks too have put in place sufficient safeguards, complied with all the rules.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will have to find out but should such an incident arise and we hope in the future, less and less of it will happen, but should such an incident arise, then, we are looking at the review to see how we can provide greater clarity on the responsibilities of both parties – the banks as well as the consumers – in order to resolve such incidents.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But certainly, we want to see fewer of such incidents and the reviews and investigations by the Police and IMDA and the safeguards that MAS is putting in place with the financial institutions will hopefully result in fewer incidents in the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First of all, my resident is also one of the victims.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Two, these are hard-earned monies, so, I am wondering whether for some of the fraud cases where the amount that is being cheated, if it is below a certain amount, can the bank just write it off first, so that it reduces the stress on the poor victims.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And thirdly, I am glad to know of the review; I am just wondering if there is an indication of the timeline for when this will be done?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Technology is fast evolving and so is the nature of crime.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, the faster we can react to this, the lesser the number of victims that we will have.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Member can file a separate question and we can always provide that data.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the second question, indeed, the banks do offer a waiver of the disputed amounts and if there are specific cases that the Member knows about, please let us know.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will be able to look at them on a case-by-case basis, raising this with the banks because, on such instances, they are prepared to offer waiver of the disputed amounts, as I have said, taking into account the individual circumstances of the victims involved.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we are doing as fast as we can.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Speaker, I am wondering if the Minister can clarify the extent to which a much more robust legislation, along the lines of what we see in terms of the Consumer Credit Protection Act of 1968 in the US, has been seriously considered and examined by MAS and the Ministry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Aljunied)
text: For those of us that have spent some time in the US, we would be aware of the enormous comfort that is provided by the kind of consumer protection legislation where, at the very least, it means that the amount of liabilities that are faced are often capped at a certain amount, once evidence of fraud has been established.
